description: Pregnancy food safety rules built only from two Australian guides. Ratings: red = avoid, amber = OK with a stated caveat, green = fine. Where the guides disagree, the rule uses the stricter advice and links to an entry in `conflicts`.

field_guide.category: Food group, matching the guides' tables.
field_guide.name: Human-readable food name.
field_guide.match_terms: Lower-case words or phrases to match against barcode ingredient lists, menu text and photo labels.
field_guide.caveat: For amber: the condition that makes it OK. For red: null.
field_guide.safe_if: For red items that become OK when prepared differently (e.g. cooked until steaming hot). Null if never OK.
field_guide.limit: Optional quantity limit, structured for the app to track.
field_guide.hazards: listeria | salmonella | toxoplasmosis | mercury | vitamin_a | alcohol | caffeine | general_food_poisoning.
field_guide.ask_restaurant: What to ask or request when ordering. Null if not relevant.
field_guide.sources: Which guide(s) say this, with PDF page number and a short paraphrase.
field_guide.conflict: Id of an entry in `conflicts` if the guides disagree on this food, else null.
field_guide.warning: Optional. true = the guides disagree and this item is only OK under strict conditions; the app should show the caveat as a prominent warning, not a footnote.

hazards.listeria: Bacteria that can pass to the baby and cause miscarriage, stillbirth or premature birth. Uncommon but dangerous. Killed by heat, so cooking or reheating until steaming hot makes food safe.
hazards.salmonella: Causes nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and fever. In rare cases can cause miscarriage. Found in raw eggs, raw sesame products and undercooked meat.
hazards.toxoplasmosis: Infection that can harm the baby's brain and eyes. Found in raw or undercooked meat, unwashed produce, raw shellfish, unpasteurised goat's milk and cat faeces.
hazards.mercury: Some large fish have high mercury which can harm the baby's developing nervous system.
hazards.vitamin_a: Retinol (a form of vitamin A) in large amounts may harm a developing baby. Liver and some non-pregnancy supplements are high in it.
hazards.alcohol: No safe amount in pregnancy. Can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, premature birth and foetal alcohol syndrome.
hazards.caffeine: Too much may increase the chance of miscarriage, premature birth or low birth weight. Limit to 200 mg a day.
hazards.general_food_poisoning: Food left out, stored too long or made by someone unwell can carry germs.

rules.name: Raw or undercooked meat and poultry
rules.safe_if: Cooked thoroughly with no pink left (mince, sausages) and clear juices (chicken, pork).
rules.reason: Raw and undercooked meat can carry toxoplasmosis and salmonella.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask for it well done / cooked right through.

sources.says: Don't eat raw or undercooked meat.
Raw meat, raw chicken, other poultry, beef, pork: DON'T EAT.
No pink left in mince or sausages; clear juices for chicken or pork.

rules.name: Thoroughly cooked meat (beef, lamb, pork, mince)
rules.caveat: Cooked right through and eaten hot. NSW gives at least 71°C. Leftovers into the fridge promptly, eaten within a day and reheated until steaming hot.
rules.reason: Thorough cooking kills toxoplasmosis and salmonella. Fully cooked meat is also a good source of iron.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask for it well done. For burgers, check there is no pink in the middle.

sources.says: Thoroughly cooked meat and chicken. Leftovers in fridge, use within 24 hours, reheat thoroughly.
Beef, pork, chicken, mince: cook thoroughly to at least 71°C (medium), eat while hot.

rules.name: Freshly cooked chicken and poultry (served hot)
rules.caveat: Cooked thoroughly (NSW: at least 74°C, clear juices) and eaten while hot. Leftovers in the fridge within 2 hours, reheated until steaming hot and eaten within a day.
rules.reason: Cooking kills salmonella and listeria. Cold chicken is a separate, high-risk item.
rules.ask_restaurant: Check it is freshly cooked and served hot, not cold or pre-sliced.

sources.says: Thoroughly cooked chicken is safe.
Home-cooked chicken: cook thoroughly to at least 74°C and eat while hot.

rules.name: Hot takeaway / BBQ chicken
rules.caveat: Only if freshly cooked and still hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours, reheat until steaming hot, and eat within 24 hours.
rules.reason: Freshly cooked, hot chicken is safe. Once it cools and sits, listeria can grow.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask for one freshly cooked and still hot.

sources.says: Hot takeaway chicken is safe if freshly cooked and still hot.
Purchase freshly cooked and eat while hot. Leftovers reheated to at least 60°C, use within a day.

rules.name: Cold cooked chicken or turkey
rules.safe_if: Reheated until steaming hot and eaten straight away.
rules.reason: Cold, ready-to-eat chicken is a common source of listeria.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask if the chicken can be freshly cooked and served hot, or pick a hot dish instead.

sources.says: Avoid cold, cooked chicken unless heated to a high temperature.
Don't eat cold meats, chicken or turkey from sandwich shops and cafes.
Cold chicken or turkey, e.g. used in sandwich bars: DON'T EAT.

rules.name: Cold deli / processed meats
rules.safe_if: Cooked until steaming hot (NSW: at least 75°C) and eaten soon after, e.g. on a hot pizza.
rules.reason: Ready-to-eat meats can carry listeria. Freshly sliced deli meat is not safer than packaged because the slicer can be contaminated.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask for the meat to be cooked hot (e.g. on a pizza or in a toastie heated through), or leave it out.

sources.says: Don't eat packaged or unpackaged ready-to-eat meats such as ham and salami unless reheated and steaming hot. Freshly sliced is not safer.
Ham, salami, luncheon, chicken meat: DON'T EAT unless cooked to at least 75°C and eaten soon afterwards.

rules.name: Processed meats cooked hot (e.g. on pizza)
rules.caveat: Must be cooked until steaming hot (NSW: at least 75°C) and eaten soon afterwards.
rules.reason: Heat kills listeria.
rules.ask_restaurant: Make sure it comes out piping hot.

sources.says: Processed meats are safe if thoroughly cooked, steaming hot and eaten soon afterwards, like on a pizza.
DON'T EAT unless thoroughly cooked to at least 75°C and eaten soon afterwards.

rules.name: Refrigerated pâté and meat spreads
rules.reason: Pâté that needs to be kept in the fridge is a high listeria risk.
rules.ask_restaurant: Leave off the pâté (common on banh mi and charcuterie boards).

sources.says: Avoid pâté that needs refrigeration before opening.
Refrigerated pâté or meat spreads: DON'T EAT.

rules.name: Canned or jarred pâté / meat or fish paste (shelf-stable)
rules.caveat: Only shelf-stable cans or jars (stored at room temperature before opening). Refrigerate after opening.
rules.reason: Canning makes it safe until opened.

sources.says: Pâté, meat paste or fish pastes in cans or jars are safe at room temperature until opened.

rules.name: Liver
rules.caveat: No more than 50 g a week, and cooked thoroughly.
rules.reason: Liver is very high in retinol (a form of vitamin A), which may harm a developing baby.

sources.says: Limit liver to very small amounts, no more than 50 grams a week.
Limit liver to 50 grams per week due to high vitamin A (retinol).

rules.name: Stuffing cooked inside chicken or poultry
rules.safe_if: Cooked separately (not inside the bird) and eaten hot.
rules.reason: NSW says stuffing should only be eaten if cooked separately from the bird and eaten hot (no reason given; it sits in the raw-poultry risk group).
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask if the stuffing is cooked separately.

sources.says: Stuffing from chicken or poultry: DON'T EAT unless cooked separately and eaten hot.

rules.name: Freshly cooked fish (most types)
rules.caveat: Freshly cooked right through (NSW: at least 63°C) and eaten hot. Recommended 2 to 3 serves (150 g each) a week (RWH says 1 to 3). Leftovers in the fridge, reheated until steaming hot, eaten within a day.

limit.note: Recommended range: RWH 1-3, NSW 2-3 serves a week.

rules.reason: Fish gives omega-3 and iodine for the baby's brain and nervous system. Cooking kills listeria.
rules.ask_restaurant: Check it is cooked through, not seared or rare.

sources.says: 1 to 3 serves of fish each week recommended.
Freshly cooked fish are safe. Serve is 150 g.
Eat 2-3 serves per week of any fish and seafood not on the high-mercury list. 1 serve = 150 g.
Cook thoroughly to at least 63°C and eat while hot.

rules.name: Shark (flake) and billfish: swordfish, broadbill, marlin
rules.caveat: No more than one serve (150 g) a fortnight, and no other fish at all in that fortnight.
rules.reason: These fish have high mercury, which can harm the baby's developing nervous system.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask what fish is used. 'Flake' in fish and chips is shark. Choose another fish if you've had fish this fortnight.

sources.says: Shark (flake), marlin, broadbill, swordfish have high mercury.
Limit to once a fortnight and don't eat any other fish during that time.
1 serve per fortnight of shark (flake) or billfish, and no other fish.

rules.name: Orange roughy (deep sea perch) and catfish
rules.caveat: No more than one serve (150 g) a week, and no other fish that week.
rules.reason: These fish have high mercury.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask what fish is used.

sources.says: Limit orange roughy (sea perch) and catfish to once a week, and no other fish during that time.
1 serve per week of catfish or orange roughy (deep sea perch), and no other fish.

rules.name: Canned fish and seafood
rules.caveat: Once opened, store leftovers covered in the fridge (NSW: use within a day).
rules.reason: Canning kills listeria. Snack-size tins of tuna and salmon are less than half a serve, so several a week is fine.

sources.says: Snack sized tins of tuna and salmon have less than half a serve and are safe to eat several times a week.
Canned seafood including smoked oysters and mussels is safe.
Canned foods: store unused portions in the fridge in clean, sealed containers and use within a day.

rules.name: Freshly cooked shellfish and crustaceans
rules.caveat: Must be freshly cooked right through and eaten hot. Not pre-cooked cold prawns.
rules.reason: Shellfish are low in mercury and safe when freshly cooked. Raw or pre-cooked chilled shellfish can carry listeria or toxoplasmosis.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask whether prawns are cooked to order or pre-cooked and chilled.

sources.says: Shellfish and crustaceans generally have lower mercury.
Freshly cooked seafood such as shellfish and crustaceans, e.g. prawns, lobster, is safe.
Cooked fish and seafood: cook to at least 63°C, eat while hot.

rules.name: Pre-cooked chilled prawns
rules.safe_if: Cooked again until steaming hot and eaten straight away (they are then freshly cooked seafood).
rules.reason: They may not be freshly cooked and can carry listeria.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask for prawns cooked fresh and served hot.

sources.says: Avoid pre-cooked prawns.
Avoid pre-cooked prawns as they may not be freshly cooked.
Ready-to-eat chilled peeled prawns: DON'T EAT.

rules.name: Raw fish and seafood
rules.reason: Raw seafood can carry listeria, and raw oysters, clams and mussels can carry toxoplasmosis.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask for the seafood cooked through, or choose a cooked option.

sources.says: Avoid uncooked or smoked seafood.
Avoid raw fish or seafood.
Raw seafood: DON'T EAT.
Don't eat raw oysters, clams or mussels (toxoplasmosis).

rules.name: Smoked seafood (chilled, not canned)
rules.safe_if: Canned smoked seafood is fine. Otherwise only if cooked into a hot dish until steaming hot.
rules.reason: Chilled smoked seafood is a listeria risk.
rules.ask_restaurant: Swap smoked salmon for bacon cooked crisp, or ask for it left off.

sources.says: Avoid uncooked or smoked seafood.
Avoid smoked seafood like smoked salmon, except if canned.

rules.name: Sushi with raw or smoked seafood, or not freshly made
rules.safe_if: RWH: freshly made sushi with no raw or smoked seafood (e.g. cooked chicken, cooked prawn, tinned tuna, egg cooked firm, vegetable). NSW: home-made only, no raw meat or seafood, eaten immediately. NSW says don't eat any store-bought sushi.
rules.reason: Raw and smoked seafood carry listeria, and sushi that sits around lets listeria grow.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask for a roll made fresh in front of you with only cooked fillings (e.g. teriyaki chicken, cooked prawn, avocado, cucumber).

sources.says: Avoid sushi with raw or smoked seafood, or sushi that isn't freshly made. Freshly made sushi without raw or smoked seafood is fine.
Eating out: avoid sushi containing raw or smoked seafood or that isn't freshly prepared.
Store-bought sushi: DON'T EAT. Home-made: don't use raw meat or seafood, eat immediately.

rules.name: Freshly made sushi with only cooked fillings
examples: tinned tuna roll made at home
rules.caveat: Not OK unless freshly made to order (or at home) with only cooked fillings and eaten straight away. Never from a display, sushi train or supermarket fridge, and no raw or smoked seafood. NSW says home-made only; RWH allows shop sushi if freshly made.
rules.reason: Cooked fillings and fresh preparation keep listeria risk low.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask for it made to order rather than from the display.

sources.says: Freshly made sushi without raw or smoked seafood is fine.
Home-made: don't use raw meat or seafood, eat immediately. Store-bought: DON'T EAT.

rules.name: Soft and semi-soft cheeses (not cooked)
rules.safe_if: Used in a cooked dish and heated until steaming hot (NSW: at least 75°C), eaten soon after, e.g. baked spinach and ricotta, hot cheese pizza.
rules.reason: Soft cheeses can carry listeria. Cooking kills it.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask for the soft cheese to be left off a cold salad, or choose a dish where it is baked hot.

sources.says: Some soft cheeses like brie, camembert, ricotta, feta and blue cheese, but soft cheeses in cooked dishes are safe.
Avoid brie, camembert, ricotta, feta, blue cheese unless used in a cooked dish.
Soft and semi-soft cheese, e.g. brie, camembert, ricotta, fetta, bocconcini and blue: DON'T EAT unless cooked to at least 75°C and eaten soon afterwards.

rules.name: Soft cheese cooked in a hot dish
rules.caveat: Heated until steaming hot (NSW: at least 75°C) and eaten soon after cooking.
rules.reason: Cooking kills listeria.
rules.ask_restaurant: Make sure it is served piping hot.

sources.says: Soft cheeses in cooked dishes are safe.
Thoroughly cooked to at least 75°C and eaten soon afterwards.

rules.name: Hard cheese
rules.caveat: Keep in the fridge.
rules.reason: Hard cheeses are low risk and a good calcium source.

sources.says: Hard cheeses are safe.
Hard cheese, e.g. cheddar, tasty: store in the fridge.

rules.name: Processed cheese, cheese spreads, cream cheese, cottage cheese
rules.caveat: Keep in the fridge and follow pack storage instructions. NSW: eat within two days of opening.
rules.reason: These are made safely but listeria can grow if kept too long after opening.

sources.says: Processed cheese, cream cheese, cheese spreads and cottage cheese (follow storage instructions) are safe.
Store in the fridge, eat within two days of opening pack.

rules.name: Paneer
rules.reason: Listed as safe by RWH. (NSW does not mention paneer.)

sources.says: Paneer is in the 'eat' list.

rules.name: Pasteurised milk, yoghurt, cream, buttermilk
rules.caveat: Check 'best before' / 'use-by' dates and follow storage instructions.
rules.reason: Pasteurisation kills bacteria. Dairy is a key calcium source (2.5 serves a day recommended).

sources.says: Milk, yoghurt, cream, buttermilk are safe.
Pasteurised milk, cream, yoghurt: check dates and follow storage instructions.
2.5 serves of dairy a day meets calcium needs (3.5 if 18 or under).

rules.name: Unpasteurised (raw) milk and dairy
rules.reason: Unpasteurised dairy can carry listeria, and unpasteurised goat's milk can carry toxoplasmosis.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask if the cheese or milk is pasteurised.

sources.says: Avoid unpasteurised milk and dairy foods.
Unpasteurised (raw) dairy: DON'T DRINK OR USE.
Don't drink unpasteurised goat's milk (toxoplasmosis).

rules.name: Soft serve ice-cream (and shakes/smoothies made with it)
rules.reason: The dispensing machine may not be thoroughly cleaned, which is a listeria risk.
rules.ask_restaurant: Choose packaged or scooped ice-cream instead.

sources.says: Avoid soft serve ice-cream and smoothies made with it, because the machine may not be thoroughly cleaned.
Soft serve: DON'T EAT.

rules.name: Fried ice-cream
rules.reason: NSW lists fried ice-cream as do-not-eat (it gives no reason; it sits with soft serve under listeria-risk dairy).

sources.says: Fried ice-cream: DON'T EAT.

rules.name: Packaged frozen ice-cream (not soft serve)
rules.caveat: Keep frozen and eat frozen.
rules.reason: Packaged ice-cream kept frozen is safe.

sources.says: Ice-cream (not soft serve) is safe.
Packaged frozen ice-cream: keep and eat frozen.

rules.name: Custard
rules.caveat: Store-bought: fine cold if freshly opened, then refrigerate, reheat until hot and use within a day. Home-made: cook thoroughly (NSW: at least 71°C), eat hot, reheat until hot and use within a day.
rules.reason: Custard is egg and milk based. Fine when fresh or well cooked, risky once it sits.

sources.says: Custard is in the 'eat' list.
Store-bought: can be eaten cold if freshly opened; use within a day. Home-made: cook to at least 71°C, eat while hot.

rules.name: Thoroughly cooked eggs
rules.caveat: Cooked until the yolk thickens / is firm (NSW: at least 71°C). Don't use cracked or dirty eggs. Keep eggs in the fridge.
rules.reason: Thorough cooking kills salmonella. Eggs are a good source of protein and iron.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask for eggs cooked hard / yolk fully set.

sources.says: Eggs cooked thoroughly until the yolk thickens.
Avoid eggs with cracked shells.
Cooked egg dishes: cook thoroughly to at least 71°C. Don't use cracked or dirty eggs.

rules.name: Raw or runny eggs
rules.safe_if: Cooked until the yolk is firm.
rules.reason: Raw and undercooked eggs can carry salmonella.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask for eggs cooked hard (yolk fully set), and for hollandaise to be left off.

sources.says: Don't eat raw or undercooked (runny) eggs.
Avoid raw or runny eggs.
Avoid foods that contain raw egg; always cook eggs thoroughly.

rules.name: Foods that may contain raw egg
rules.safe_if: Made with store-bought, shelf-stable mayonnaise/aioli, or cooked thoroughly.
rules.reason: Raw egg can carry salmonella.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask if the aioli, mayo or dressing is made in-house with raw egg. If so, ask for it on the side or swapped for a non-egg sauce.

sources.says: Avoid foods that may contain raw eggs: mousse, eggnog, home-made mayonnaise, aioli, Caesar salads in restaurants, uncooked cake batter.
Avoid homemade and cafe-made mayonnaise which may contain raw eggs.
Raw egg in food, e.g. home-made mayonnaise, aioli, chocolate mousse, cake batter, pancake batter: DON'T EAT.

rules.name: Store-bought mayonnaise and aioli (commercial)
rules.caveat: Commercial jar/bottle only. Refrigerate after opening and follow storage instructions; check use-by / best-before dates.
rules.reason: Commercial mayonnaise is made to be safe. Home-made or cafe-made may use raw egg.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask whether the mayo is house-made or from a commercial jar.

sources.says: Store-bought mayonnaise is safe if kept in the fridge and storage instructions followed.
Non-refrigerated commercial mayonnaise, aioli: check dates, follow storage instructions.

rules.name: Dips containing feta or ricotta
rules.reason: Uncooked soft cheese carries a listeria risk.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask if the dip contains feta or ricotta.

sources.says: Avoid dips that contain feta or ricotta cheese.

rules.name: Raw sesame products: tahini, hummus, halva, sesame paste
rules.reason: Raw sesame products have been linked to salmonella.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask for no hummus or tahini sauce (common in kebabs, falafel, shawarma and Middle Eastern plates). Garlic sauce may also contain tahini, so ask.

sources.says: Avoid raw sesame seeds and their products, including tahini, halva and hummus.
Avoid sesame products made from ground or whole sesame seeds like tahini, halva and hummus.
Hummus, tahini and any other sesame paste, store-bought or home-made: DON'T EAT.

rules.name: Heat-treated sesame: sesame oil, seeds baked on bread
rules.caveat: Only when the sesame has been heated or baked.
rules.reason: Heat treatment makes sesame safe.

sources.says: Sesame seeds that have been heat treated are safe to eat.
Sesame products that have been heated, like sesame oil and seeds on baked bread.

rules.name: Pre-prepared or pre-packaged salads (incl. coleslaw and fruit salad)
rules.safe_if: Freshly made just before eating from well-washed ingredients.
rules.reason: Salads that sit around can grow listeria.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask if the salad is made fresh to order. Avoid buffets and salad bars.

sources.says: Avoid coleslaws, salads and fruit salads unless you're sure they're freshly prepared.
Avoid pre-prepared salads from salad bars or smorgasbords.
Pre-prepared or pre-packaged salads including fruit salad: DON'T EAT.

rules.name: Freshly made salad
rules.caveat: Wash ingredients well just before making. No raw sprouts. Eat fresh; leftovers into the fridge and eaten within a day.
rules.reason: Washing and eating fresh reduces listeria and toxoplasmosis risk.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask for no sprouts, no soft cheese, and no house-made egg dressing.

sources.says: Freshly prepared salads, except those with raw alfalfa, bean sprouts or snow pea sprouts.
Home-made: wash ingredients well just before making and eating; use leftovers within a day.

rules.name: Sprouts (bean sprouts, alfalfa, snow pea sprouts, etc.)
rules.safe_if: Cooked thoroughly (NSW: not raw or lightly cooked).
rules.reason: Sprouts can carry salmonella and listeria.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask for no sprouts (common on pho, pad thai, banh mi, poke and sandwiches), or for them to be cooked in the dish.

sources.says: Avoid sprouted seeds such as alfalfa, bean sprouts or snow pea sprouts unless thoroughly cooked.
Don't eat any type of sprout, whether raw or lightly cooked.
Bean sprouts: DON'T EAT raw or lightly cooked.

rules.name: Fresh vegetables and herbs
rules.caveat: Wash well before eating raw or cooking.
rules.reason: Washing removes soil that can carry toxoplasmosis. Leafy greens are rich in folate and iron.

sources.says: Fresh cooked vegetables (wash before cooking).
Wash well just before eating raw, or wash before cooking.

rules.name: Canned and frozen vegetables
rules.caveat: Frozen vegetables should be cooked, not eaten straight from frozen or uncooked (NSW). Canned: follow storage instructions after opening.
rules.reason: Frozen vegetables are not a ready-to-eat food and can carry listeria if not cooked.

sources.says: Canned and frozen vegetables are in the 'eat' list.
Frozen vegetables: cook, don't eat uncooked.

rules.name: Whole fresh fruit
rules.caveat: Wash before eating.
rules.reason: All whole fruit is safe once washed.

sources.says: All types are safe except store-bought pre-cut fruit. Wash whole fruit before eating.
Whole fresh fruits: wash well before eating.

rules.name: Store-bought pre-cut fruit
rules.reason: Pre-cut fruit can grow listeria, especially rockmelon.
rules.ask_restaurant: Avoid fruit platters or fruit salad unless cut fresh to order.

sources.says: Avoid store-bought, pre-cut fruit, especially rockmelon.
Pre-prepared or pre-packaged salads including fruit salad: DON'T EAT.

rules.name: Rockmelon (cantaloupe), whole and cut at home
rules.caveat: Not OK unless bought whole, the skin washed before cutting, cut at home and eaten fresh. Never pre-cut, from a fruit salad or platter, or from a cafe. NSW says avoid rockmelon altogether; RWH allows it this way.
rules.reason: Rockmelon is a listeria risk, especially when pre-cut. The guides disagree on whole rockmelon, so it is only OK under these strict conditions.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask for no rockmelon in fruit salads or platters.

sources.says: Buy whole rockmelon and clean the skin before cutting. Avoid store-bought pre-cut fruit, especially rockmelon.
Rockmelons: DON'T EAT.

rules.name: Freshly squeezed juices and smoothies from cafes / juice bars
rules.safe_if: Made at home from washed whole fruit and drunk straight away.
rules.reason: They use pre-cut fruit, and juicing machines can be hard to clean (listeria).
rules.ask_restaurant: Choose bottled pasteurised juice or a hot drink instead.

sources.says: Avoid freshly squeezed juices and smoothies from cafes and juice bars because they use pre-cut fruit and machines can be hard to clean.

rules.name: Pre-prepared or pre-packaged sandwiches and wraps
rules.safe_if: Made fresh to order with safe fillings (no cold deli meat, cold chicken, soft cheese, sprouts or raw-egg mayo), or toasted until steaming hot.
rules.reason: Food made more than a day in advance can grow listeria, and common fillings are high-risk.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask for it made fresh, or toasted until hot. Skip deli meats, cold chicken, soft cheese, sprouts and house mayo.

sources.says: Avoid any foods that may have been made more than a day in advance, e.g. pre-made salads, sandwiches and wraps.
Pre-prepared or pre-packaged sandwiches or wraps: DON'T EAT.
Don't eat cold meats, chicken or turkey from sandwich shops and cafes.

rules.name: Freshly cooked restaurant or takeaway food
rules.caveat: Choose food that is freshly cooked and served steaming hot. Check the individual ingredients against the other rules.
rules.reason: Hot, freshly cooked food has very low listeria risk.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask that it is served piping hot.

sources.says: Choose food that is freshly cooked and make sure hot food is steaming hot.

rules.name: Salad bars, smorgasbords, buffets and food stored for a long time
rules.safe_if: Food cooked fresh and still steaming hot.
rules.reason: Food that sits out or has been stored a long time can grow listeria.
rules.ask_restaurant: Choose dishes cooked to order.

sources.says: Avoid refrigerated, ready-to-eat foods that may have been stored for a long time.
Avoid pre-made food if you think it's been stored a long time, and salad bars and smorgasbords.

rules.name: Cooked leftovers
rules.caveat: Refrigerate as soon as it stops steaming, covered. Eat within 24 hours (a day), reheated until steaming hot (RWH: 74°C for 2 minutes; NSW: at least 60°C). Or freeze and reheat later.
rules.reason: Listeria can grow slowly in the fridge. Reheating until steaming hot kills it.

sources.says: Cook or reheat until steaming hot, at least 74°C for 2 minutes, and eat straight away.
Eat leftover foods within 24 hours and reheat them until steaming hot.
Store leftovers covered in the fridge, eat within a day and always reheat to at least 60°C.

rules.name: Fridge food left out at room temperature
rules.caveat: Eat within 2 hours of coming out of the fridge. NSW: don't eat if it's been out 2 hours or more. RWH: preferably within 2 hours, definitely within 4; throw out at 4+ hours. App default follows NSW (2 hours).
rules.reason: Bacteria grow quickly at room temperature.

sources.says: Eat fridge food as soon as possible, preferably within 2 hours and definitely within 4 hours. 4+ hours: throw it out.
Eat cold foods within 4 hours of preparation, unless they've been refrigerated.
Don't eat food that's meant to be in the fridge if it's been left out for two hours or more.

rules.name: Canned and bottled foods
rules.caveat: After opening, store leftovers in a clean sealed container in the fridge (NSW: use within a day).
rules.reason: Canning makes food safe until opened.

sources.says: All are safe, just follow the storage instructions after opening.
Store unused portions in the fridge in clean, sealed containers and use within a day.

rules.name: Soy products
rules.caveat: Check best-before / use-by dates and follow storage instructions.
rules.reason: All soy products are safe.

sources.says: All soy products like tofu, soy milk and soy yoghurt are safe.
All soy products: check dates and follow storage instructions.

rules.name: Bread, cereals, rice, pasta, noodles
rules.reason: Recommended staple (about 8.5 serves a day, mostly wholegrain). Most Australian bread (not organic) is fortified with iodine and folic acid.

sources.says: Grain foods 8.5 servings a day, mostly wholegrain.
Most breads except organic are fortified with iodine.
Most breads and some cereals have added folic acid.

rules.name: Nuts, seeds, legumes
rules.caveat: Cook legumes. Sesame is the exception (see sesame rules).
rules.reason: Good sources of protein, folate and iron.

sources.says: Meat, fish, poultry, cooked eggs, nuts, seeds and tofu are part of a healthy diet.
Cooked legumes such as chickpeas, lentils, kidney and lima beans are iron-rich.

rules.name: Alcohol
examples: desserts or sauces with uncooked alcohol
rules.reason: No amount of alcohol is safe in pregnancy. It can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, premature birth or foetal alcohol syndrome.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask for a mocktail or alcohol-free option.

sources.says: Best to avoid alcohol completely. No amount is safe during pregnancy.
Safest option is not to drink if pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding (NHMRC).

rules.name: Energy drinks with caffeine or guarana
rules.reason: Contain caffeine or guarana (another caffeine source).

sources.says: Energy drinks like Red Bull and V contain caffeine or guarana. Best not to have these.
Avoid energy drinks with guarana or caffeine such as V, Red Bull, Mother.
Avoid drinks marked as sports or energy drinks that contain caffeine.

rules.name: Coffee, tea, cola, hot chocolate (caffeine)
rules.caveat: Keep total caffeine under 200 mg a day: about 1-2 espresso-style coffees, or 3 instant coffees, or 4-5 cups of tea, hot chocolate or cola. Avoid double-shot espresso (NSW).

equivalents.tea_cup: 4 cups medium strength (NSW) / 3-5 or 4-5 depending on strength (RWH)

rules.reason: Too much caffeine may increase the chance of miscarriage, premature birth or low birth weight. Caffeine also reduces iron absorption.
rules.ask_restaurant: Ask for a single shot, or decaf.

sources.says: Limit caffeine to 200 mg per day: 1-2 espresso, 2-3 instant, 3-5 tea, hot chocolate or cola.
200 mg per day: 1-2 espresso, 3 instant, 4-5 tea, hot chocolate or cola.
Limit to 200 mg daily: 1-2 espresso, 3 instant, 4 medium tea, 4 cocoa/hot chocolate. Avoid double shots.
Caffeine in tea, coffee and cola reduces iron absorption.

rules.name: Artificial sweeteners
rules.caveat: Safe in moderation. (Note: diet cola still contains caffeine.)
rules.reason: RWH says artificial sweeteners are safe if used in moderation.

sources.says: Artificial sweeteners are safe if used in moderation.

rules.name: Non-pregnancy multivitamins and vitamin A supplements
rules.caveat: Use a pregnancy multivitamin (contains safe beta-carotene). Check regular multivitamins with a pharmacist, and talk to a doctor before taking any supplement.
rules.reason: Regular multivitamins may contain retinol; too much vitamin A can harm the baby.

sources.says: Pregnancy multivitamins contain safe beta carotene. Regular multivitamins might have retinol; check with your pharmacist.
Talk to a doctor or dietitian before taking supplements. Too much vitamin A can be a risk to the baby.

conflicts.rwh: Buy whole rockmelon and clean the skin before cutting; only pre-cut is to be avoided (p6).
conflicts.app_default: amber with warning: not OK unless whole, washed, cut at home and eaten fresh. Pre-cut stays red (rule fruit-pre-cut).
conflicts.note: Decided by Sas 2026-11-02: stricter rule, but shown as amber with a warning caveat rather than red.

conflicts.nsw: Store-bought sushi: DON'T EAT. Home-made only, no raw meat or seafood, eat immediately (p12).
conflicts.rwh: Freshly made sushi without raw or smoked seafood is safe (p5, p7).
conflicts.app_default: amber with warning: not OK unless made to order with only cooked fillings and eaten straight away. Display, sushi train and supermarket sushi stays red.
conflicts.note: Decided by Sas 2026-11-02: stricter rule, shown as amber with a warning caveat. Both guides agree raw or smoked seafood sushi is red.

conflicts.nsw: Reheat to at least 60°C until steaming hot (p10, p12).
conflicts.rwh: Cook or reheat until steaming hot, at least 74°C for 2 minutes, to kill listeria (p2).
conflicts.app_default: Use 'steaming hot all the way through' in plain text, and show 74°C for 2 minutes where a number is given.
conflicts.note: Both say 'steaming hot'; only the number differs.

conflicts.topic: How long fridge food can sit out
conflicts.nsw: Don't eat if left out for two hours or more (p10).
conflicts.rwh: Preferably within 2 hours, definitely within 4; throw out at 4+ hours (p2). Cold foods within 4 hours of preparation (p7).

conflicts.app_default: Show 2-3 serves (150 g each) as the target, with up to 3. Not a safety conflict.

conflicts.topic: Cups of coffee/tea that equal 200 mg caffeine
conflicts.nsw: 1-2 espresso, 3 instant, 4 medium tea, 4 cocoa/hot chocolate (p11). Avoid double-shot espresso.
conflicts.rwh: Page 1: 1-2 espresso, 2-3 instant, 3-5 tea/hot chocolate/cola. Page 7: 1-2 espresso, 3 instant, 4-5 tea/hot chocolate/cola. (RWH differs from itself.)
conflicts.app_default: Track mg where known (e.g. barcode). For cups, use the lower counts: 1 espresso-style coffee or 2 instant counts as roughly half the daily limit.
conflicts.note: All agree on the 200 mg/day limit.

conflicts.nsw: All soft and semi-soft cheeses, naming brie, camembert, ricotta, fetta, bocconcini and blue (p13).
conflicts.rwh: Brie, camembert, ricotta, feta, blue cheese (p2, p5). Does not mention bocconcini/mozzarella.
conflicts.app_default: Use NSW's broader 'soft and semi-soft' scope, incl. bocconcini and fresh mozzarella.
conflicts.note: Not a contradiction, NSW is broader.

conflicts.nsw: Pre-prepared or pre-packaged sandwiches or wraps: DON'T EAT, regardless of filling (p7, p12).
conflicts.rwh: Avoid cold meats, chicken or turkey from sandwich shops and cafes (p4); no blanket ban on pre-made sandwiches.
Canned and frozen vegetables are fine (p6), no mention of cooking.
conflicts.app_default: amber: cook frozen vegetables before eating.

conflicts.nsw: Store unused portions in the fridge in clean sealed containers and use within a day (p12).
conflicts.rwh: Follow the storage instructions after opening (p7).
conflicts.app_default: Within a day, in the fridge (NSW).

conflicts.nsw: Beef, pork, chicken, mince: cook thoroughly to at least 71°C (medium), eat while hot (p12). Also: no pink left in mince or sausages (p10).
conflicts.rwh: Thoroughly cooked meat only; don't eat raw or undercooked meat (p4).
conflicts.app_default: Rare and medium-rare red. Medium or more amber for whole cuts of beef/lamb (cooked to 71°C). Mince, sausages, burgers, pork and chicken must have no pink.
conflicts.note: Not a direct contradiction; NSW is just more specific.

handling_tips.tip: Wash your hands before preparing or eating food, and after gardening or handling pets.
Use separate clean chopping boards and knives for raw and cooked food.
Keep the fridge below 5°C. Keep eggs in the fridge. Cover stored food.
Keep raw meat on the bottom shelf so juices don't drip onto other food.
Thaw and marinate food in the fridge or microwave, never on the bench.
Refrigerate hot food as soon as it stops steaming.
Boil marinades that held raw meat before serving them.
Use a food thermometer if you can.
Don't eat past the use-by date. If in doubt, throw it out.
Avoid food made by someone who is sick (e.g. with diarrhoea).
Wear gloves for cat litter and gardening.
Shop with a cooler bag; take an esky on picnics.
When travelling overseas, avoid tap water. Don't swallow lake or river water.

nutrition_notes.note: Folic acid supplement of at least 400 micrograms a day from a month before pregnancy through the first three months. Folate-rich foods: green leafy vegetables, broccoli, chickpeas, nuts, orange juice, dried beans and peas, fortified bread and cereals.

27 mg a day. Iron-rich: lean beef and lamb, poultry, fish, iron-fortified cereals, eggs, cooked legumes, dried fruit, green vegetables. Vitamin C helps absorption; caffeine reduces it. Only take iron supplements on a doctor's advice.
1000-1300 mg a day; about 2.5 serves of dairy or calcium-fortified soy (3.5 if 18 or under).
Higher needs in pregnancy. Most non-organic Australian bread is iodine-fortified; some women need a supplement, so ask a doctor, midwife or dietitian. Fish also provides iodine.
From fish; important for the baby's brain and nervous system.

disclaimer: General information only, based on the two listed guides. It is not medical advice. For advice specific to you, talk to your doctor, midwife or obstetrician.
